title: References and borrowing
summary: Lend a value instead of giving it away, under rules the compiler checks.

blocks.html:
The last chapter ended on a problem: handing a String to a function gave it away for good. The fix is to lend it instead. A reference is a pointer to a value that somebody else still owns, and the compiler tracks the loan from beginning to end.

&T is a shared reference. It reads the value without taking it, without copying it, and without ever freeing it. The owner at the call site does not move.

blocks.title: borrow instead of take

blocks.html:
Two marks do the work: &String in the signature says the parameter is a borrow, and &name at the call site says we are lending it. Inside the function, s is used exactly like a string — s.len() just works.

When measure returns, the loan is over and s ceases to exist. name never lost ownership, no heap bytes were touched, and the last line prints both values. That is the whole trick: nobody paid for a copy.

blocks.title: change it through a borrow

blocks.html:
A mutable reference is written &mut T. It lets the borrower change the value in place, so the owner must be declared mut, and the call site writes &mut to make the borrowing visible. Changing data through &mut is free: the string is edited where it already lives.

Now the rule that follows. At any moment, a value has either any number of shared references &T, or exactly one mutable reference &mut T. Never both at once, and never two mutable at once. That single sentence is what the borrow checker enforces.

blocks.title: many readers, or exactly one writer
blocks.ascii:
fine: many readers at once
     &s -->\
            +--> [ "hi" ]   owned by s
     &s -->/

  fine: one writer
     &mut s -------> [ "hi" ]   nobody else is looking

  refused: a writer joins the readers
     &s -->\
            +--> [ "hi" ]
     &mut s ------>  ^ cannot borrow as mutable

blocks.html:
Write the refused case and the compiler quotes the rule back at you:

error[E0502]: cannot borrow `s` as mutable because it is also borrowed as immutable
|
3 | let a = &s;
| -- immutable borrow occurs here
5 | let c = &mut s;
| ^^^^^^ mutable borrow occurs here
6 | println!("{a} {b} {c}");
| - immutable borrow later used here

Two mutable references get their own number, E0499: cannot borrow `s` as mutable more than once at a time. The motivation is not bookkeeping. A reader holding a pointer while a writer grows the string is a use-after-free in C; here that state simply cannot be written down.

blocks.title: sequential is always fine

blocks.html:
That compiles, and it is not a special case. A borrow lasts until its last use, not until the end of the block. a is used on the third line and never again, so the shared loan ends there; the mutable loan on the fifth line begins with nobody reading. Restricting access in time rather than in code shape is what makes the rule livable.

The other half of the guarantee is that a reference can never outlive its value. If you try to return a reference to a local variable, the compiler answers error[E0515]: cannot return reference to local variable `s` — the value dies with its function, so the loan would dangle. Rust refuses to compile it instead of hoping you notice.

References also let us talk about part of a value. Index a string with a range and prefix it with & and you get a slice: a reference to those bytes, with no copy made. The range is half-open, so 0..2 means bytes 0 and 1. &word[..] is the whole string as a slice.

A slice of a string has type &str — a pointer and a length that own nothing. It supports .len() just like &String does, and it is what every well-behaved Rust function asks for when it only needs to read text.

blocks.title: slices, and handing one back

blocks.html:
None of that is magic. The compiler has been tracking who owns which bytes since the first line of the chapter, so it knows that part may read the two bytes word owns, that first_two may hand back a slice of its input because the input outlives the loan, and that nothing needs cloning.

Practical habit, then: if a function only needs to read a string, take &str. If it needs to change one, take &mut String. Take String only when you really want to keep it. Almost nothing you write in the rest of this book needs the clone that the last chapter forced on you.

quiz.q: What does the parameter type in fn measure(s: &String) mean for the caller?
options: The function reads the string and the caller keeps ownership
The function takes ownership and frees the string
The string is copied into the function
quiz.why: &String is a shared borrow: a pointer the callee may read through. The owner keeps the value and no bytes are duplicated.

quiz.q: Which situation does the borrow checker reject?
options: Two shared references in use at the same time
A mutable reference and a shared reference in use at the same time
A shared reference used, finished, then a mutable one
quiz.why: The rule is any number of shared references or exactly one mutable reference, never both at once. Sequential borrows are fine because a borrow ends at its last use.

quiz.q: With let mut s = String::from("hello"); what is the value of &s[0..2]?
options: A &str slice that points into the existing bytes
A new String that owns a copy of "he"
The two characters as a tuple of char
quiz.why: A slice borrows a range of the original bytes. It is a pointer plus a length, it owns nothing, and its type is &str.

exercise.brief: Write add_bang so it pushes one '!' onto the end of the borrowed string. Then call it twice on text in main and print the result.
exercise.hint: Inside add_bang, s is already a mutable borrow, so s.push('!'); is enough — no asterisk, no reassignment. At the call site you must pass &mut text.
